title: The State of Alabama / The State of Nick Saban
dek: Alabama has to prove its football again. Saban is trying to influence what college football becomes.
body:
The dynasty did not disappear. It changed tense. Alabama enters Kalen DeBoer's third season after an 11-4 year, an SEC Championship Game appearance, a road playoff win at Oklahoma, and a 38-3 Rose Bowl loss to Indiana. The school extended DeBoer through January 2033. This is his program now, not a waiting room for a closer Nick Saban replica.

The largest question is quarterback. Austin Mack is the older system adult; Keelon Russell is the younger creator. Neither has started a college game. Alabama's secondary already looks like the roster's clearest strength, while the offense still has to settle two line positions and prove it can move a good defensive front when the run is expected.

Saban remains retired from coaching. His regular football work is with ESPN, and he has publicly supported DeBoer's handling of the transition. His more consequential new role is political: he testified for the Protect College Sports Act, backing legitimate NIL earnings while calling for national rules, transfer stability, agent oversight, health protections, and a limit on disguised pay-for-play. The counter-read is included: institutional stability also returns control to powerful programs and adults, and the SEC itself opposes the bill's current form.

A light SEC primer places Alabama sixth inside a five-team playoff crowd separated by only 90 preseason-media-poll points. Georgia and Texas own the cleanest lane. Alabama's season turns on Georgia, Tennessee, Texas A&M, and LSU—and on whether the new quarterback makes the offense coherent after the first call fails.
